column121: Aircraft X was in a storage state during preservation maintenance when an engine run was accomplished on both #1 and #2 engines with their main oil tank empty and their respective main accessory gearbox drained of oil as well. This is an event that is unprecedented; I am here to focus on how serious this is in regards to determining serviceability of the subject engine(s). As an experienced lead AMT; I am no stranger to engine overhaul; test cell duties; diagnostic test flights or on-wing engine/taxi runs. I know how violent an engine reacts when it incurs an internal failure while in operation and to summarize the thought process; it's fortunate that many of these failures happen on the ground during maintenance but some unfortunately happen when an aircraft is in service and in flight.Every engine manufacturer designed these engines to operate normally on different phases of flight under different conditions providing that the operator/consumer; observes; adheres to all or any operational instructions provided. In regards to engine oil quantity; our company pre-run checklist; before an engine is even operated; it must contain a minimum of 1X quarts of main oil quantity as displayed in the flight deck. I have no doubt that an engine will still operate normally with lesser quantity if oil pressure and oil temps remain normal and no other abnormal parameters are observed. If an anomaly does happen during an engine operation that's related to oil and or lubrication system; especially those observed readings that can indicate an impending failure or incursion beyond its operating limits; the engine in operation must be stopped immediately. The company has ample resources available to address or troubleshoot these issues in the form of MMs; FIMs; TSMs; etc.; and likewise; all modern aircrafts has built in systems known as recorder mediums such as PCM; DMU; and FLT RCDR that can be downloaded as necessary to provide insight and health assessment to many operating parameters including engines at real time or recorded. With the issue we have; none of the recording mediums downloaded has provided us with any source of readings and or indications that may shed light as to how we can possibly approach and deal with this problem. Here's the issues that I have: These engines were run with no oil in tank and main accessory gearbox oil was drained as well. With the rate of speed that these engines operate even at idle; there are many parts within the scope of the lubrication systems that is dependent on proper oil pressure in order to maintain normal operating temp such as the huge thrust bearings; sideload bearings and other compartment bearings along with the other critical parts like the scavenge and pressure pumps. Common sense will also dictate that with no oil to begin with; these bearings and critical seals have now been exposed to undetermined excessive heat that may have inflicted heat damage and reduce life cycle on other parts. I have thoroughly searched the MM and TSM in hopes to provide me some insight on how to troubleshoot or address this issue and found none. In fact; due to my curiosity; I have checked all the other fleets troubleshooting manuals and was unsuccessful as well. The only fleet that came close to addressing an oil pressure issue involves the CFM engines and that's whenever its engine oil pressure goes below minimum limits that exceeds 30 seconds; the engine is to be replaced. Engines are just not designed to operate with the oil system drained and it's beyond my scope of knowledge and experience to determine serviceability. Unless an engine manufacturer can provide us insight; recommendations or have experienced a similar event and shares us the information and or make known to us what decision that had to be made; we and the Company is in a serious predicament. What we are being asked as part of the maintenance process are these EG callouts that instructs to check MCDs and perform numerous engine runs as to ascertain and prove its serviceability. These engine runs are unfounded and lack merit and frankly speaking; they are very dangerous. They clearly appear experimental; based on assumptions and not ECRA supported. These proving engine runs are best authorized and done in a test cell environment where it is safe and properly managed. In summation; these engines were not run with a low oil qty condition as many may have thought or have been misled to think. One would argue that it still had oil in the form of residuals in the lines and that would be enough to come to a conclusion that all the bearing compartments and other critical areas were not affected or heat damage is not a factor. These types of arguments are foolish and obviously do not share the same mindset as I and that is to operate with a mindset that's geared towards safety; legality and have a high degree of confidence that the right decision is made; without any doubts or reservations. The public views us as an airline of choice and as we transport them around; they expect guaranteed reliability; safety and comfort. In conclusion; the decisions to be made hinges on two different paths. One is to render the engine serviceable after maintenance proving runs that is unfounded; lack merit or support from many technicians and frankly speaking; the engine(s) are damaged goods! The other direction is to follow the only recourse that should have been in the first place. Stop these foolish maintenance practices that may prove dangerous downline and do what's right.

column121: After watching a demo of fogging the aircraft for possible viruses with a new procedure I had noticed that the fog would enter into the forward and aft cabin temp sensor module. The fog is a wet fog that coats the surfaces to disinfect. The fog will easily enter the module that are in the PSUs. The power for these comes from your P6-4 power panel and controlled from your 115v AC bus that is still powered with your ground service bus. These Temp sensors have had issues in the past on all fleets with dirt and dust coating the sensor and giving false reading of cabin temp. Example; the pilot write up might say Aft cabin temp hot or cold this is due to the temp bulb dirty in most cases.  This is a procedure we are doing and we had talked about this to the others that were giving the demo of our concerns. Also with the smoke detectors in the cabin and cargo. There are similar systems on several aircraft types that operate in the same manner.   Either pull the circuit breaker in the systems before you spray the cargo or cabin or clean the sensors after spraying the cabin and or cargo in accordance with the manuals. This would avoid any delays to the aircraft departure and discomfort to our passengers and cabin crew members due to any delays or hot or cold cabin temps or false smoke warnings.

column121: This morning; I was told to troubleshoot a BLEED 2 Fault caution message deferral on an ERJ 175. [I] interrogated [the] CMC (Central Maintenance Computer) and found codes that were flagging the high stage bleed valve and the nacelle pressure regulating shutoff valve as two of the major faults. Troubleshot per FIM 36-XX-XX-XXX-XXX but was having difficulty figuring out [the] effectivity of aircraft software version. Found effectivity and troubleshot accordingly. Performed Bleed 2 TM (Technical Manual) Controller IBIT (Initiated Built-In Test) both channels and the check passed. The discrepancy was signed off as a transitory condition per FIM 36-XX-XX and the valve was un-deferred.After paperwork was done; the Supervisor and I revisited the issue and decided it was smart to run the engine to make absolutely sure the issue was resolved. While trying to engage the RH (Right Hand) engine bleed air system; the BLEED 2 Fault caution message came back into view; flagging the NAPRSOV (Nacelle Pressure Regulating Shutoff Valve) - the valve that was supposedly deferred before troubleshooting started. The aircraft was needed for dispatch so I consulted Inspections/Quality Control about fixing paperwork to allow for the valve to remain on deferral instead of clearing the deferral like originally intended. They said they'd try and later told me to create a non-routine write-up for the troubleshooting work performed and [to] carry forward the original deferral due to lack of time; aircraft needed for dispatch. I did said paperwork and re-deferred what I thought was the NAPRSOV referencing MEL 36-XX-XX; with MEL 36-YY-YY accompanying it as a requirement to apply MEL 36-XX-XX; but I didn't notice that it was in fact not the NAPRSOV to begin with but the high stage bleed valve that was deactivated initially. Due to paperwork and system issues; Contract Maintenance was called out to the aircraft at a different base to verify the maintenance action being correctly complied with and found the wrong valve deferred. I was in a rush due to the aircraft being needed for dispatch and flustered with the complexities of troubleshooting this issue. I looked up the deactivation process for the NAPRSOV but accidentally overlooked the fact that it was the aft valve not the forward one like I had thought it was. [Some suggestions could be] possibly labeling the valves somehow; such as a metal placard and band that can be taken off and installed on a new valve in the event that it needs to be changed. A toolbox talk would be nice to spread awareness of the different places of the valves. Due to the part numbers of both the NAPRSOV and the high stage bleed valve being the same; the only difference in function is where they're installed on the aircraft; which happens to be almost right next to each other. Though; that being said; now that I think about it the AMM isn't unclear about it in the first place; so I can't really blame unclear paperwork. ALSO a toolbox talk about where to find epic load and CMC LDI software versions on an ERJ 175 would have helped as well.

I then called the on duty Coordinator and was informed the AMT's were enroute to [the spot] to accomplish the nose gear inspection. The AMT's arrived on [the spot] at XX:45 hrs and noticed the damage to the R/H nose gear door linkage as well as minor damage to the R/H nose gear door and called Aircraft X not airworthy. The aircraft was then taxied under power to [the spot] and the aircraft was called [out of service] at that time. The aircraft was later repositioned to the hangar for repairs.This event occurred due to the fact that the ramp crew pushed out an Aircraft X on [the spot] incorrectly thus damaging the nose gear door and nose gear door linkage. The Ramp Maintenance Director then informed Operations Control and Hangar with false information which started some confusion of the airworthiness of Aircraft X on [the spot].Re-train the ramp crews the correct way to accomplish the push out of the aircraft. Inform the Ramp Maintenance Director not to inspect aircraft of suspected aircraft damage or to inform the Hangar or Operations Control whether an aircraft is airworthy or not. Leave it for the licensed aircraft mechanics. The Hangar and Operations Control will no longer accept information from the ramp or Maintenance Director regarding aircraft damage. column121: During my shift [I] was tasked to complete slat adjustment on #11 slat. A few hours in it was noticed that the outboard target on the auxiliary track was not lining up with its sensor. A quick glance at the adjacent slat seemed to confirm that the targets were not in the correct position. Being under pressure to get the aircraft out we swapped the positions and pressed on with the adjustment test without doing our due diligence and verifying with the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual). Several hours later we were about to lose the 2nd shift inspector for the night so we had to rush to catch up paperwork for his stamp before he left for the night and we continued on with the 3rd shift. At that point we were so focused on the adjustment steps we had done we forgot about the target swap and failed to document it. Had we remembered; the improper installation would have been caught and corrected and this problem never would have occurred. We continued on with adjustments for several more hours doing sensor gap checks and PSEU/FSEU (Proximity Sensors Electronics Unit/Flap Slat Electronics Unit) electrical checks that all passed.We were under incredible pressure to get the plane out. Because of a lack of training and ability in our 1st and 3rd shifts; we were not allowed to turn any of this work over to them and so [that day we] were pressured to work it until it's done. [A] lack of accountability in some members of all shifts who only give the bare minimum of effort translates into a lot of pressure put on just a few leading to poor morale; fatigue and lack of focus that translates into mistakes. Being told that we have to get the majority done so that the next shift only has to worry about putting on panels because 'they don't know how to do it' is getting to be a frustratingly common occurrence. It leads to [having] tunnel vision on getting the job done that critical steps get missed. Things like just catch the paperwork up at the end so you can keep your momentum become standard instead of documenting as you go. Even when things outside of our control occur; inflexibility in the deadline and an 'it is what it is' attitude conveyed from above keeps the pressure on. This check was no different in that a ramp incident with our next AC (Aircraft) dropped it here ahead of schedule; so there was no give on our launch date even with some late findings and when it was obvious we weren't going to make it was just time to turn up the heat. Day 1 of a new check isn't much better as we are told to work as much as possible early to avoid the crunch; but then we do not receive a lot of our required parts until the end of the check. So no matter what we always feel behind.[I suggest] first; better training on all shifts so work like this can be continuously worked instead of left to only one group. That could have a big impact on the pressures of being rushed at the end of every C check.  Second would be real accountability for underperforming staff who by lack of effort are putting more work on others. Everyone pulling equally would improve moral and lead to less crunch at the end of a C check. [Another suggestion is] better [and] timelier sourcing of parts/materials to once again; better space our work flow so we are not always up against it at the 11th hour. These things would go a long way to reducing the stress that impacts morale and invites mistakes.  Another thing would be to place a large emphasis on mechanics using partial sheets as they are intended to be used. We tend to get complacent about just working and catching the paperwork up at the end and this leads to things being missed or forgotten. Individual mechanics making the entry at the time the inspector witnesses a step and having it bought then will eliminate the possibility of things being missed or forgotten.
column123: We were in a time constraint to get the airplane out; and noticed that one of our slat targets was loose. We copied the target locations on slat 10 and swapped targets on 11 to mirror 10. We tested our gaps and even did a near far test on our targets to make sure that they were in the right place working properly. Upon arrival it required an ETOPS pre-departure check; engine oils serviced; and an MEL for CABIN INTERPHONE INOP to be cleared and [a] restoration [of] the aircraft's [Maintenance Release]. As soon as the aircraft arrived at Gate XX; Maintenance received a call from Ramp notifying us that there was something sticking out of from the left-hand wing just above #1 Engine Pylon. I knew they were talking about the speed tape that Tech Support and I installed for a write-up we cleared earlier that day.Routinely; I go directly to the Flight Deck to do my ETOPS inspections and take note of engine oil quantity. Per the Task Card; everything was in order and I radioed my Lead asking for a lift and some speed tape for the wing. While waiting for him; I ran some tests and cycled various circuit breakers in an attempt to clear [the] CABIN INTERPHONE message on the center aisle Tuning Control Panel (TCP). The message did not go away and I didn't have enough ground time to troubleshoot further. I would have to 're-defer' this MEL later.Once I finished the inside; I went downstairs when my Lead called me over. He was on the lift and told me he will return with the wider roll of speed tape. I said okay; I will join after I have accomplished servicing the engine oils and doing my walk-around. I grabbed the 3 engine oil cans I needed and continued to service the #1 Engine which only needed 1 QT. After filling up the #1 Engine I moved on to Engine #2 which needed 2 QTS. Once finished; I stored the used cans and did my walk-around. Finally; I went back upstairs to the Flight Deck to ensure the engine oil levels were sufficient and they were.While in the Flight Deck; I planned on waiting for the flight crew so I could brief them about the INOP CABIN INTERPHONE message on the TCP that I was going to 're-defer.' In the meantime; I decided to keep attempting to troubleshoot. It was my first experience with the 787 dealing with a system fault which failed to show up on the EICAS Status Page. Usually any little discrepancy would be displayed on the status page. My theory is perhaps it was because the interphone was still functional. I kept trying to think of anything I could do to just get rid of the INOP message on the TCP.My time was up when the flight crew arrived. After briefing them about the issue; I joined my Lead who just finished up with the wing. He had me go up on the lift to verify the speed tape installation and it was satisfactory. We finished up at the gate and returned back to the office. I signed off all of the assigned work for the aircraft. [The] ZZZ Planner assisted us with the 're-defer' on the MEL and I issued the aircraft's [Maintenance Release]. Later on that day; I received a phone call from my Manager informing me that Aircraft X had to divert to ZZZ1 due to excessive loss of oil from the #2 Engine. It was [in] that moment [that] I realized I may have been too distracted from the other workload [to] properly secure the filler cap on the oil tank.

column121: I; Mechanic A and Mechanic B were assigned 2 aircraft; Aircraft X and Aircraft Y. This scenario was out of the norm as we are usually assigned 1 aircraft per night. The reason this is abnormal is because the job for the night was an 'Entry to Park' card for Aircraft X and an 'Entry to Park' and a 'Return to Service' card for Aircraft Y. It was clear from the initial job assignments that these cards are taken very lightly and are considered nuisance cards or at least that is how they appeared. Aircraft X was assigned a XI:10 am trip and Aircraft Y was assigned a XG:30 am trip. The assignments were issued between XI:30 and XJ:00 pm. I myself have not entered an 'Entry to Park' AC and had many questions about the process as these airplanes were already at or beyond 48 hrs. on the ground. We were told to place Aircraft X into parking and leave it and to park and return to service Aircraft Y. This created much confusion for us on Aircraft Y. How do you park and return to service an aircraft immediately? Why are these cards issued now? Why the lack of manpower? What did they expect from us? How do we even accomplish these task in such a short amount of time? Do we have the ability to [apply] N/A to boxes? How did these surpass the clock? If we have to drain the water system and deactivate the heaters where are the planes parked to refill and reactivate? What equipment is available to get up to the tail and how far to get it there? Is there garbage on the airplane and do we have to dump it as per the card? Do we have to cover the pitot [tubes] only to take the tape off immediately? What airplane is the priority; the early out (because different parking spots indicate different abilities)? Why did safe go into maintenance mode when we were reviewing safe? Why did our ability to print the Procedures Manual go out for a half hour? Who do we contact; as the card suggested? Because management didn't have the answers for the questions we asked; I made two attempts to call Tech Services and the company phone dropped off and I had to use my cell and then that dropped off. The clock was ticking we made a choice to start with the aircraft on the gate after we found its location because it was going into parking and staying for dayshift. This gave us time for people to come back with the answers we needed to know about putting an aircraft into parking and taking it out immediately and how to handle. Normally we would have started with the early out aircraft. Mechanic A felt the pressure with comments such as they are going to expect these airplanes. My reassurance to him 'don't worry we just do our best' wasn't enough and he made a stand move alone while myself and Mechanic B were in the cabin and hit Aircraft X taking that airplane out of service with a 2.5 by 2.75 dent on the frame. The team was disheartened to say the least and we notified management immediately. After they arrived; Mechanic A was very distraught. I let them know that we did not even get to Aircraft Y yet and asked if they have an answer and what was the expectation for that plane. The answer was no answer yet; and yes they still expect that plane. This was around XA:30 to XB:00 am. So with that we finished off Aircraft X and the entry to park then we went to lunch very late; way past our union contract time. When I got back from lunch; all the paper work I had printed to start the next aircraft was removed from the east office and in some type of transportation mode so all the work was missing. Looking for the work brought us around XD:30 am and still could not locate it. End of shift was XE:30 and so we abandoned any potential work to be done on Aircraft Y. What is their expectations to accomplish an Entry to Parking and a Return to Service in a single night just for the sake of accomplishment with no real positive outcome other than to risk a failure?The cards need to be made more realistic or the company needs to be more realistic about their flight schedulesand actual workload. This whole program of parking needs to be revamped. This whole process left more questions than answers and different interpretations. It's a real mess in my personal opinion and in some cases may lead mechanic who has a work efficiency outlook to do it way different (some would say cut corners) than a mechanic who has a processes outlook and will park the plane before lunch then would return to service after lunch wasting materials and supplies and filling landfills simply because they realize that is the process.
column123: I was assigned to work 2 airplanes Aircraft X required an Entry to Park and Aircraft Y required Entry to Park and required to Return to Service. I worked alongside Mechanic C and Mechanic B. We had many issues with this job being with the workload and their expectations it seemed to be a lot. We didn't receive any direction and it didn't seem to make sense but we tried to comply as the best we could. I know they wanted the airplanes in the morning but I didn't see how we can do it without taking some shortcuts. Their expectations seemed high. We did our best. I was working as fast as I can to help keep up with the other 2 mechanics. I had to move a stand to cover the pitot probes and I was moving the stand around the aircraft. Having such a large workload; I felt pressure to move the stand on my own. I am always willing to help others without question; but sometimes when I bother people to help with stands; they cause a conflict and I don't really like to cause or have conflicts at work as it stresses me out. Many times if I ask for help it creates more problems so I try to be independent. As I was pushing a stand; there was an air conditioning hose in the way and I turned off the power and flattened the hose. I probably should have disconnected it; now that I look back; but at the time I have done this before as I observed other mechanics do and as I went over the hose I fell the stand got away from me because of the weight and it hit the plan. I regret the decisions I made even though they seemed okay at the time I guess the pressure got to me. I have to learn to deal with the pressures placed on me. I will seek advice as suggested by steward to talk to the Employee Assistance Program to help me tackle this. I think the workload was unfair and the expectations were high. I should have removed the hose and I should have had a spotter. There were many variables. I also believe the stand should have a better bumper placement as that alone would have helped tremendously if not eliminated [the risk] with certainty.

column121: An aircraft had an air return for the loss of number 1 engine; green; hydraulic pressure; no loss of fluid. The aircraft was moved to the hangar on day shift for repair. We motored the engine and observed the pressure coming from the pump: it increased to 3000 psi then fell off. The aircraft was moved inside and the cowlings were opened up for inspection of the EDP (Engine Driven Pump). There were no external leaks or external damage to the EDP. We continued to inspect the fluid lines from the pump to the pylon disconnect. It was found that the fluid supply line had become disconnected at the pylon connection; it was further noticed that the locking section of the pylon side of the fluid supply line quick disconnect was not locking to the line side. column121: I was told to go to the gate at ZZZ airport to inspect a write up on an ERJ175. The write up stated that the pilots were not able to get cool air in the cockpit during cruise; but the packs worked and blew cool air on ground. It was written up previously and was a repeat write up. Because this was a repeat and there were no EICAS (Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System) messages reported; I decided to interrogate the CMC (Central Maintenance Computer) for active faults and faults stored on the previous flight. I found two fault codes on the current leg as active with no inactive time stamp showing it was resolved. I then went to active faults and both codes were stored as active there as well. The two fault codes were 21000020AM2 and 21000030AM2. Following the FIM (Fault Isolation Manual); the problem was a fault with SPDA (Secondary Power Distribution Assembly) 2 Module 26. I inspected the MEL (Minimum Equipment List) list and there was no deferral for this item. I informed my lead and ordered parts needed for repair. The parts would not arrive until the next morning so I was told it would be days. Shortly after arriving at work; I was informed that it was signed off as left pack deferred and flew out. Looking at the fault codes; the fault was for more than just the pack system which made it non-deferrable.Days did not follow the turn over stating that the faults were active and that the problem was with the SPDA 2 Module 26. They also did not look up fault in FIM and followed the procedures. This allowed for a broken plane to have a different part to be deferred while the actual problem was not addressed. Mechanics need to follow manuals and carefully read shift turnover.

column121: I want to take the opportunity to express my concerns regarding pitot tubes covers and inspection requirements and that is...here at ZZZ we have airplanes that sit on ground for more than XX hours and therefore need pitot inspections before departure as the GPM XX.XX.X states and are accomplished...our concerns rely on the fact that these same airplanes are not scheduled to depart until most of times well beyond a substantial period of time on ground and as mechanics we feel that signing the pitot inspections well before hours (i.e.; 4 hours; 6 hours; 8 hours; etc.) before departure is a safety concern because these same aircrafts are sitting on remote pads of the airport without pitot covers since ZZZ has no covers available or NOT enough!! We cannot have; for safety reasons; mechanics signing pitot inspections when airplanes are not scheduled to depart for another 5 or 6 hours until departure time...what guarantees that bugs or other forms of FOD is not gonna get inside those tubes after having signed for the inspections in the AML Logbook??  We have brought this issue with ZZZ management but they tend to believe that because the GPM XX.XX.X states 'Before Departure;' this 2 word sentence to them means: 'ANY time the Aircraft is linked in [the system]'...which we STRONGLY DISAGREE...since again departure times are well beyond the 6-8 hours before departure.  We as maintenance Mechanics would be in jeopardy of putting our licenses on the line if something was to happen with pitot systems after signing for the inspection and still have aircrafts sitting on ground for another 6-8 hours uncovered.  We strongly recommend the GPM XX.XX.X be revised with specifics regarding Pitot Inspections and sign offs.  I want to thank the many individuals in your department for keeping us informed with updated info on issues that pertain to aircraft maintenance.  We hope that this particular issue gets resolved for the sake of everyone in maintenance and our flying public.These events are recurrent.GPM needs to be specific about their definition of 'Prior to departure.'  We strongly suggest the inspection be performed with aircraft on gate prior to departure (2 hours) and notate it in AML log.
column125: Mechanic reported that after pitot inspections are accomplished prior to departure; aircraft frequently sit on the ground for hours with no pitot tube covers to protect against contaminants.

column121: This is a SAFETY concern. In order to issue the B737 MEL 35-XXX for the Passenger Oxygen Complete System inop; Boeing MEL 'M' procedure; step 'e' requires portable oxygen units to be provided for at least 10% of the passengers. Our 737 NG aircraft is configured for 160 passengers. If we multiply this number by 0.10%; [it] is equal to 16 portable oxygen units that are required to be in compliances with the MEL instructions. During the last MEL Rev 60-XX; a note was added to the 'M' procedure for clarification. This note reads the following. 'The B737 NG is equipped with sufficient portable oxygen CAPACITY to provide for 10% of the passengers; provided that no more than one bottle is inoperative or missing.' The information provided on this note contradicts the 'M' procedure and requirements to issue this placard. The 737 NG is not equipped with sufficient portable oxygen units for 10% of the passengers in accordance with our emergency equipment configuration. There are only 6 portable oxygen units available in the cabin for the passengers. The amount of oxygen available for the passengers should not be measured based on the CAPACITY of oxygen available in the aircraft; but the AMOUNT of units available to assist multiple; different passengers in the event of an emergency.This MEL is a SAFETY hazard for our passenger and flight crew; and should be corrected as soon as possible due to compliances.

column121: Pressurized brakes...It did it again. It was not even X years ago that I landed a Piper Malibu on a short runway only to notice upon touchdown that one complete side of the brake system was completely inoperative. Now; just last week; it happened again. Here's the story; and Piper needs to fix to the design problem...The Malibu has inverted master brake cylinders on the rudder pedals like many Pipers. Normally; the brakes work and there are no problems. Yet an insidious problem will develop. There are 3 O-rings on each master cylinder and these O-rings will leak. Yet; they will not leak brake fluid out of the system; they will and do let air into the system. The Malibu is pressurized; and when flown with a differential cabin pressure; the pressure is pushing air in to the brakes system thru the brake master cylinders. The cabin air which is under pressure is flowing to any opening in the cabin which to escape. When the O-rings in the brake system allows the cabin air to enter the braking system; the brakes stop working. If allowed to persist; the air in the system renders the brakes on the affected side or both sides ineffective...or even non-existent.Upside-down brake master cylinders...As you would expect; the air migrates upwards and enters the brake lines even so insidiously and it doesn`t take much air to make the brakes disabled. Here's the issue; Malibu brake failures are common on flights where the brakes worked perfectly on run-up and pre flight checks. The problem does not reveal itself until the brakes are used on landing.Although the checklist in the Malibu clearly states to check the brakes prior to takeoff. How do you check the brakes in flight prior to landing?If either side of the braking system is weak or non-existent; perform a go-around and consider your options. Pilot might want to fly to an airport with a longer runway if they have fuel. They may want to fly an approach a little slower and maybe plan to touch down as early as practicable on the runway. They might want to call for safety vehicles to be ready in case there is a landing over run issue and notify the FAA. In any case; you do not want to touch down on the runway and then realize you've got a brake problem. Many Piper pilots and passengers are in danger when this occurs.

column121: A rotorcraft was in a all metal hanger with all doors closed except one with a 5 ft. walk through space. The aircraft was undergoing a FAR part 91. 411 413 static & transponder 24 month test. The aircraft is also ADS-B (aircraft dependent surveillance broadcast) equipped with a Lynx NGT9000 plus transponder (ads-b in and out). We had performed this test on numerous aircraft in the past in the same location within the building to contain the transponder altitude signal as the test aircraft altimeter system was raised to perform the required testing. No problems with outside aircraft either in the pattern for the airport or overflying the area were ever noted or reported. In the time period between the last aircraft test and this one; the airport had installed an additional ADS-B surveillance radar site. No notification was sent to any operators and we were not informed by the administrator. During the 91.411 / 413 testing; the new radar equipment received the ADS-B data and it was routed into the national airspace system automaticaly. The next day; we received a call from our FSDO (Flight Standards District Office) concerning a possible deviation by a commercial air carrier to a traffic conflict alert generated by the ADS-B system. The conditions were VFR but ATC advised the carrier of the presence of the test aircraft even though it was on the ground in a metal hanger.There should be a provision ; either through a phone contact with ATC to provide a ' test ' window for performing this type of aircraft maintenance with the registration number being posted on the ads-b data as an aircraft under test or other nomenclature. Possibly a software change to allow a maintenance function to be displayed through the ADS-B broadcast that would alert other aircraft that this particular ADS-B report is in fact not an airborne aircraft. Due to the sensitivity of these airport surveilance radars; it was found by phone calls to other operators; that this is a problem that is recurring around the country. The ramp test equipment has provisions to contain the transponder signal; but the effect of RF (Radio Frequency) leakage is not guaranteed.

This will prevent any accidental deployment.

column121: We had walked into the hanger that morning and found out that we were doing an engine change. The engine had already been removed and needed to be installed. My Supervisor was the one in charge of the operation and he had wanted us hang the engine on the FWD top mount first then the AFT mount and then the bottom FWD mount. The task has you install the AFT mount 1st and then the 2 FWD mount; but since I had worked with him before on engine installs I just followed his lead. We had got the 1st mount installed on the aircraft we ran into some trouble on the AFT mount. We had ended up damaging both the upper and lower cowling and 2 hinge fitting panels. Later I had found out that the 2 panels were supposed to be removed before the engine ever can off the plane. We ended up pulling the engine back off aircraft and on removal the engine had snapped down and had made a small nick on the FWD mount. My other Supervisor (who was working with us the whole time) was trying to tell me that the damage was no big deal when I knew that the FWD mount had no damage limits. I had ended up writing up the damage to all 3 parts that got damaged.I believe that the damage to the aircraft could have been prevented if the 2 panels had been removed and we had followed the task in order. There should also be note in the task stating that the AFT mount needs to go in 1st. I also believe that supervisors shouldn't be doing the work of the mechanics. They seem to have a time ordinated mentally over a safety one.
column123: On DATE on first shift at the ZZZ maintenance hangar; the right engine of aircraft X was being installed by the first shift maintenance crew. The individuals who performed and assisted in the task and include; myself (NAME2 RII Inspector); NAME (Maintenance Supervisor); NAME1 (Maintenance Supervisor); NAME3 (Maintenance Lead); NAME4 (Maintenance Technician); NAME5 (Maintenance Technician); NAME6 (Maintenance Technician); and NAME7 (Maintenance Technician). NAME8; Assistance Chief Inspector was also a witness to some portions of the task being performed. During the installation of the right engine the upper trans cowling 443AT; the lower trans cowling 443AB; and the upper and lower rear thrust reverser hinge line fairings 443BT and 443BB were damaged. Also there was damage to the forward engine mount on the pylon side. NAME (Maintenance Supervisor) was taking the lead on the job and operating the heavy duty forklift. Of the employees performing the task NAME had the most experience in doing this specific engine CF34-8C5 installation. NAME6 was the only technician besides NAME who had performed the specific installation task before and he had only performed it one time. Before the job started there was a safety meeting to discuss the possible dangers of the job. Everyone was assigned a position on the lifts; on the aircraft pylon; or on the ground. NAME8 present at the safety meeting and shortly thereafter I saw him from a distance talking to NAME about the task giving him some advice on how to install the engine and to make sure the task was followed exactly. Since I was on the lift and carrying out other duties I did not hear much of the conversation but it seemed more like an argument. NAME8 left the job site and we began to hoist the engine in place. NAME directed the mechanics to install the forward engine mount first because it was easier. NAME mentioned to us all that he had done at least five successful engine changes this way with no issues. At this point no one made an objection this. The two mechanics on the engine pylon; NAME4 and NAME5 aligned the forward engine thrust mount into place and torqued and safetied the nuts and bolts. They then attempted to align and fit into place the aft thrust mount. After a few minutes of trying the aft thrust mount would not fit into place. At that point myself and NAME6 double checked the manual instructions which we had on hand on the lift. We mentioned to all that the aft thrust mount should have been installed first according to the instructions the manual laid out. NAME stated that it should not matter and they proceeded to try again to fit the aft thrust mount into place. NAME3 kept saying that he thought some thing was binding where he was in the front side of the engine pylon. He mentioned this several times but because we were all in different positions around the engine we could not see was he was talking about. NAME3 asked NAME specifically if the panel 443BT is supposed to come off because it seemed like it was in the way. NAME replied that he had never seen that panel come off in his experience. They proceeded for another few minutes and then decided to remove the engine from the aircraft and put it on the stand to double check if anything was wrong with the engine mounts on the engine side. After the engine was secured on the stand. We found the above mentioned aircraft damage. A few minutes after the damage was discovered we did some more research. We found that the technicians that removed the engine the day before on second shift failed to remove panels 443BT and 443BB that are specifically mentioned in the removal task. We believe that this was the cause of the damage to the aircraft. With the panels installed there was not enough room to position the engine in place correctly. As an R.I.I. I rejected the installation in the maintenance software program and the maintenance staff asked for engineering relief for the damage. NAME then refused to sign the AMM task even though he took the lead on the job and operated the engine lift thereby performing undocumented maintenance on the aircraft.There were many factors that contributed to this incident. One was a serious lack of experience with this specific task. At other airlines they have an engine installation and removal team the handles all engine changes because of the complexity of the task and the teamwork it takes to do the job with five or more individuals. Most of the tasks frequently performed at ZZZ are done individually or with one helper. Only one technician on the job had performed the task more than one time. The complexity of the task meant that all involved had to read and understand a greater amount of technical data in a short period of time. Also the order of installation instructions were not followed because the most experienced technician claimed it was easier to perform the instructions out of order safely. Human factors also was a cause of this incident. The supervisor taking the lead on the job; NAME; has a reputation at ZZZ for being cocky and having a know it all 'one up you' personality. I have noticed that he has a condescending leadership style and likes to be condescending to his employees to make himself look good. Rather than train his people and build his employees up he would rather tear them down to make himself look better. I have been at Company almost six years and unfortunately Company management is full of people like NAME. I believe this creates a work environment that is intimidating and detrimental to open communication. People like NAME create a 'shame' environment where people are afraid to speak up when something is done wrong or doesn't look right to them. This creates and enhances human error.  Failure to read and understand the entire task and remove all the panels on the list for the removal task CRJ 900 AMM 71-00-00-000-801-A02-PSA led to the 2nd shift mechanics failing to actually remove the required panels. Failure to follow the installation order of specified steps in the task may have led to error also.More training by experienced technicians on more complex and team oriented task to train inexperienced technicians. In the manuals special notes to identify where the order of installation is a must and cannot be deviated from.(example: Note - Aft Thrust mount MUST BE INSTALLED prior to forward engine mount to avoid damage to aircraft and engine.) Better Leadership training for Supervisors with less than 3 years experience to avoid the cocky and condescending 'know it all' leadership culture. Make Maintenance Supervision and leadership responsible and accountable for the maintenance they perform on all Company aircraft. No running away and only making the mechanics on the floor sign something off when the job is not done right and something is broken.

column121: Incident / Discovery: Maintenance work light / flash light found in the the nose landing gear wheel well which resulted in an air return of the aircraft.Aircraft location: Aircraft X B737-800 was located in the parking area at ZZZ Airport.Work Conditions: Night time; outside; no spot lighting or ambient lighting. Sky conditions clear. Temperature 30(s) Fahrenheit.On the night; Coworker and I were assigned to troubleshoot log X 'Unable to access APU bite' Per previous log entry of being suspect; I replaced the R735 relay in the J20 box; took us some time to locate the J20 box and the relay because the WDM and IPC were not clear on the exact location. 2-3 hours to locate on aircraft. This junction box is located behind the L/H rear pressure panel of the nose landing gear box structure. However; access was difficult to the box from the nose landing gear area due to the angle of access and aircraft height. In turn; I climbed into the E/E bay with a blue hand light; head lamp and a No. 2 Philips screw driver; maneuvered/positioned myself over the flight deck air supply duct along the left side of the nose wheel box structure to get better access to the J20 cover; Relay 735 and associated cannon plug for troubleshooting purposes. Coworker was in support from the nose landing gear wheel well to hand me various items I needed to work through the access structure.As documented in the log; the relay did not correct the issue so we continued to troubleshoot which required continuous access to the J20 box. I was mainly working from inside the E/E bay; not from the nose landing gear wheel well.As the night progressed and not finding any faults with the physical wiring; we reported to our lead where we were at. Was told that the aircraft is needed for a flight; document where we were at and close up the aircraft.We headed back out to the aircraft. When we got back to Aircraft X; I double checked the APU ECU security; checked the aft cargo bay for equipment and tools; closed the aft cargo bay door. I then proceeded into the E/E bay to secure the J20 box cover and check for security and check for tools and equipment. As I was doing this; Coworker was securing the nose landing gear wheel well pressure panel.After Coworker finished installing the panel; I went inside the flight deck to re-engage two circuit breakers and to pressurize the aircraft for the leak check of the pressure panel. Once pressurized; Lead performed the leak check of the pressure panel. When leak check was satisfactory; I depressurized the aircraft; powered down; closed the main cabin door and pulled the air stairs. Shortly after we met in the vehicle we had and began going over paper work.Coworker and I are somewhat new to avionics and have a lot to learn about the various differences between our fleet types and associated details of each. We are very capable of doing the work but would feel more comfortable to be paired with someone who is well seasoned in the avionics shop. It should be this way for anyone that is new. Since I have been in the shop; I have been paired mainly with inexperienced technicians who are learning the same way as I am; learn as you go. Common sense would dictate to pair a very experienced tech with a inexperienced tech; this promotes growth; development and prevents mistakes.I'm sorry that this unfortunate mistake took place and is an oversight I strive to never let happen; unfortunately it did. I will be much more vigilant in the future about tooling and equipment used for aircraft maintenance to make sure this will never happen on my end again.

column121: My Recommendation: Because there is what I believe to be a low but uncertain chance that the primary pressure vessel of the Aircraft X has a current active failure; the aircraft should be immediately grounded; and an investigation be initiated into whether this issue is just a classification and engineering oversight; or indeed a failure to the aircraft's primary structure. Aircraft X (Boeing-767-300) is potentially operating on an inapplicable airworthiness sign off and may fly (already has flown) with a possible serious defect to the aircraft's primary structure (pressure vessel). Aircraft X arrived at ZZZ station December 2020. Upon arrival the following defect was found and recorded into the maintenance log book:Discrepancy: Undocumented Speed tape found concealing stripped & unsecured mounting screw to extruded Main Cargo Door (MCD) Manual Vent Door Drive (Pressure Vessel) cover panel.I notified Maintenance Control of the defect and submitted via email a proposal for a temp repair utilizing non-standard substitution parts available on-hand at our station that I hoped would allow for a timely repair keeping the aircraft on scheduled revenue flights despite the need for an Engineering Order (EO) and additional authorizations. After an appropriate time; an outline of maintenance action to be completed was submitted to our station for a yet unapproved EO numbered: XXXXXXXX; that was a substantial deviation from my own earlier proposed temp repair. This EO after performing a Detailed Visual Inspection (DVI) merely called for reattaching the panel in place with RTV-106 sealant; no hardware; and a covering of multiple layers of aluminum speed tape. Knowing that an external application of tape over a hole in the primary pressure vessel of an aircraft did not meet the basic criteria for acceptable maintenance standards; I contacted maintenance Control to inform them that we (aircraft technicians under my purview) at ZZZ would not be able to comply with the EO maintenance instructions as they were currently written because of the safety implications.After expressing my unwillingness to press forward with the draft EO I began receiving pressuring communications from various maintenance controllers; maintenance duty managers; and Company management; saying everything from 'just do it;' to 'it'll be fine.' Additionally; it was overheard in background talk on more than one phone call with maintenance controllers that they did not believe the panel in question was actually a primary pressure vessel fitting as I had asserted in multiple emails and phone conversations; and was merely a weather seal. Worried that I had somehow made an egregious mistake about the panel in-fact being a pressure hull seal; I enlisted both additional night shift mechanics to assist with a cabin pressurization leak check (referencing AMM 05-51-24-782-001) with the damaged MCD Manual Drive cover panel removed. As I operated the cabin pressure manually; utilizing APU bleed source; the two assisting technicians reported a strong; unrestricted flow of air emanating from the uncovered hole; while I was observing only 1 PSI indicated differential cabin pressure. Believing that this observation adequately supported my previous assertation; I terminated the test; returned the aircraft to its previous configuration; and felt confident that my continued refusal to repair the aircraft as outlined in the draft EO to be a safe and correct judgment call.The scheduled departure of the aircraft was altered from XA:15z to XE:00z. At XB:16z I received an email asking me to 'please call In to Maintenance Control to advise on current status of approved EO compliance;' (no approved EO had been received or transmitted to anyone at ZZZ station). Given the ongoing pressure from phone calls and condescending emails to comply with an EO I had yet to see; I advised [the] maintenance controllers that I would not be complying with the EO and to direct all future communications to be in writing. I then suggested at that point that they 'just AOG (aircraft on ground) ship the required parts necessary to return this defect to its original condition;' with the observation 'that the original undocumented speed tape repair has already been proven to fail;' as my own justification for non-compliance with an EO that called for doing the same thing; only with more tape.At XD:50z we received the first approved copy of the EO XXXXXXXX via email from the Maintenance Manager; which upon review was consistent with the advised sealant and tape repair already rejected. The scheduled aircraft departure was once again pushed back to XG:00z; well after the scheduled arrival of the oncoming maintenance day shift. At XE:15z I received a phone call from my Company Regional Manager asking me why I was not complying with the EO and then; regarding taping over a hole in the pressure vessel; to 'explain how this is a safety concern?' After briefly elaborating to him about how the loss of cabin pressure makes flight crews go to sleep and planes to become lawn-darts; he said that I would 'have coverage in terms of liability because the engineer signed off on three layers of speed tape.' After mutually disagreeing; he proceeded to switch the subject to asking me which maintenance technicians were coming in on day shift; then; seeming unsatisfied; continued to ask me about the status of other technicians not scheduled for shift. Several minutes after hanging up; another call was received from a subordinate technician; not scheduled to come in; inquiring as to what was going on and why the Regional Manager was asking him to come into work on his weekend and 'override' us. At the advice of another technician overhearing the conversations; I took a written note of the above quotes from the calls.With continued inquiries for resolution on the aircraft; the oncoming day shift Lead informed Maintenance Control that the EO was still unworkable as it was and reiterated that the original temp repair proposal forwarded to Maintenance Control that included substituted hardware installation would be a fix deemed acceptable and believed conforming with standard practices that we would still be willing to sign off on. Giving in; the Maintenance Controller agreed to get the hardware installation added to a revised version of the EO along with an additional step for a cabin pressurization check that the day shift Lead smartly felt necessary for repairs performed on the pressurized structure of an aircraft. With assurances that the revised EO would include the agreed upon amendments; the day shift Lead and myself expedited the repair to the aircraft in an effort to make the scheduled departure pending timely receipt of the revised EO. The cabin pressure leak check of the repair was then successfully accomplished with only a small movement observed in the repair at a peak indicated differential pressure of 4.5 PSI; and no leaks or excessive loss rates noted. Upon departing the aircraft to accomplish paperwork closeout we were greeted by the oncoming flight crew; who had apparently been kept apprised of the ongoing situation and wanted to personally thank us for looking out for their safety.At XF:18z we received the approved EO XXXXXXXX Revision 1. Required paperwork was completed; signed log pages were sent; flight crew was briefed; and the aircraft was returned to green status at XG:10z. The aircraft subsequently blocked out of the gate at XG:39z for a delay from scheduled departure of 39 minutes. Why is this a safety concern? Upon later realization and review; I have found several possible deviations to Federal Aviation Regulations (FARs); the airline General Maintenance Manual; and uncertainty to the validity of the accomplished repair that should be investigated immediately as it may represent a serious safety issue to the aircraft. Having been so narrowly focused on getting the point across to the necessary parties involved in the tribulations of Dec Xth that the damaged part was indeed part of the pressure vessel of the aircraft and that a workable repair would have to be tailored to the additional physics involved with that part of the structure; I failed to realize the broader implications of what a repair to the pressurized structure of an aircraft entailed in terms of adherence to regulations; maintenance policy; and accepted practices. The FARs define 'Primary Structure: is that structure which carries flight; ground; or pressurization loads; and whose failure would reduce the structural integrity of the airplane.' Even though steps were added to Revision 1 of the EO to conform the repair to acceptable practices 'equal to its original or properly altered condition;' because the installation hardware was a reasonably close approximation of the original parts; the additional step of adding three layers of overlapping speed tape is in direct contradiction to the airline General Maintenance Manual policy for its use:          -HIGH SPEED ALUMINUM TAPE-          High speed tape is a convenient material for use as an interim repair for          non-structural materials. Under no circumstances will it be used on primary          aircraft structure. A Log Book entry is required when high speed tape is           applied unless instructed to do so by an EO with DER approval.Under this policy; the use of speed tape in this manner is strictly forbidden and forgiveness when it comes to doing the maintenance under the provision of an EO only absolves the requirement of a log book entry for its use. However; even though agreement was made in Revision 1 of the EO for addition of attachment hardware and an added cabin pressurization leak check; the EO creator did not alter the original classification of the repair to acknowledge that the repair was in-fact being accomplished on an aircraft primary structure:          'The Main Deck Cargo Door Manual Vent Door Drive Cover is considered secondary          structure. The time limited repair per this EO is minor; and the temporary           repair per Part 1 does not affect the fit; form or function of the skin.'I would imagine this to be an oversight; and if it is; then an additional revision needs to be made which would at a minimum alter the category of the defect deferral and its associated time-limited re-inspections and permanent repair due date/cycles. If this is not an oversight; however; as this EO has been twice over reviewed and approved; and the MCD Manual Vent Door Drive Cover is indeed a secondary structure; then the original investigative cabin pressure leak test failed for a reason other than indicated (i.e. there is an existing failure of the primary pressure vessel somewhere internal to the Main Cargo Door). Which would in turn mean that a damaged secondary structure is now fulfilling the function of a primary structure pressure seal. I do not believe this to be the case; but; as the MCD is a modification from the original aircraft structure; the existing reference material available for my use to confirm the hypothesis that the cover plate is indeed a primary structure component is vague and uncertain. Tech Engineering likely has additional references not available at a line station that could perhaps shed light on the issue.Since issuing equivalent versions of the above safety report to both Airline and Company on [the next day]; Aircraft X has remained on a regular flight schedule with recurrent re-inspects per Part 2 of EO XXXXXXXX Rev 1; until receiving Part 3 Permanent Repair [4 days later]. I can currently find no record that any further investigation has been conducted.

column121: On [Date 1]; I was reviewing paperwork on the current Aircraft X in the [Maintenance Visit] in ZZZ and noticed that a robbed transponder on Aircraft X was installed the previous night and did not get a signoff in the logbook releasing the aircraft for RVSM (Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum) operation. This aircraft was still scheduled to be in the [Maintenance Visit] for another 5 days so I just had the nightshift avionics tech complete the entry the next day. But I knew that the avionics tech that forgot the RVSM signoff on the [Maintenance Visit] also replaced a transponder on Aircraft Y during the overnight on [Date 2]. The ZZZ Avionics tech that replaced the transponder is [Name].Found during paperwork reviewShould of; but did not realize the transponder is RVSMCalled Maintenance Control and had the system deferred (RVSM)[Parts Document] lists the PN (Part Number) of the transponders that go on our aircraft that are post ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) mod. This PN [XXX] is not listed in the aircraft IPC (Illustrated Parts Catalog); so there is no statement (RVSM Critical Item) like all the other transponder PN's listed in the IPC. This statement (RVSM Critical Item) should be added to the [Parts Document]; to bring attention to it like the PN's listed in the aircraft IPC.
column123: On [Date 2] I was assigned to clear a Transponder #2 MEL (Minimum Equipment List) on Aircraft Y. I determined it needed a new transponder; however; we did not have the proper transponder in stock required for ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast) mod aircraft. I was directed to rob the transponder from Aircraft X which was the [Maintenance Visit]; after robbing (from Aircraft X) and installing (on Aircraft Y) the transponder; I went through the operation checks and everything was good. I went to sign off the paperwork and seen; from the beginning of Chapter 34 in the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual); that it was not CAT II (Category 2). I forgot that RVSM (Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum) isn't included in the beginning of ATA (Air Transport Association) chapters and since I picked the part number based on [Number] I didn't see the RVSM reminder note seen in the AIPC (Aircraft Illustrated Parts Catalog). I went to open the GMM (General Maintenance Manual) on the tech computer I was using and it wouldn't open. It was known within the base that PDF's can act up on the 2 provided tech computers. My ignorance of not remembering that RVSM wasn't included in the beginnings of ATA chapters; and not going into AIPC; and assuming that since RVSM wasn't downgraded it wasn't an RVSM component; along with my laziness of not confirming with a lead or Supervisor on their computers contributed to missing the RVSM release sign off. The plane made at least one flight with out having the RVSM release. The next night I installed new transponder in Aircraft X and Operations checked everything and since I assumed it wasn't RVSM the day before I repeated my mistake for the [Maintenance Visit on Aircraft X]; and didn't write up a RVSM release sign off. It was caught before the aircraft left and the other avionics technician went through the operation checks again and provided the RVSM release sign off.The day shift Supervisor caught the [Maintenance Visit] not having the release and knew that I did the aircraft the night before and seen that I didn't release that one either and took corrective action.I didn't put max effort into looking into seeing if the component was RVSM critical. I went off of a handful of assumptions and didn't double check with my leads or Supervisor. The [Number] didn't reiterate it was an RVSM critical item; the GMM PDF didn't want to load on the tech computers; RVSM isn't located at the beginning of ATA chapters like CAT II and RII (Required Inspection Item) are.Put RVSM in beginning ATA chapters like CAT II and RII. Add a reminder in [Number] that the transponder is RVSM critical component. Remove old transponders from stock that can't be used with ADS-B aircraft seeing that our whole fleet has ADS-B mod. column121: Due to the nature of wearing a mask due to COVID-19; it contributes to a couple safety concerns.  It is a matter of time before there is a serious injury or damage due to the policy of wearing a mask the entire time while on airport property.  I have been involved in a couple of close calls and have seen issues with my coworkers as well.First off; the communication issues.  We already have issues with radio communication and I know there have been reports filed in the past for this.  However; now there is another issue involving the wearing of masks and trying to understand what the person is trying to say.  The voice is usually muffled or broken up and hard to understand.  Most of the time requiring the person receiving the transmission to ask the other person to either repeat or in some cases just misunderstands the call.  Throw in the inherent environmental noises from jet engines or air conditioning packs and other loud noise; communication becomes very difficult at times.  As you can imagine; this can easily become a safety issue especially in times of urgency or clearing of flight control movement or other tests and engine runs. Second; visual impairment.  The wearing of masks impairs your line of sight looking down.  In order to actually see the ground in front of your feet; you need to actually bend your neck down to move your head to see and while you are looking down with your head down; then that is when you end up walking into something.  You are unable to just look down.  The obstruction has caused many trips due to the obstacles of power cords; tow bars; tools; steps on ladders; walking in cargo pits; and weather related issues; such as ice and snow.  These are just a few of the most common items; but the list is endless.Also; when wearing safety glasses or prescription glasses or sunglasses; there is the issue of them constantly fogging up.  Especially in colder weather.  This just compounds the issue with not being able to see what is in front of your feet.The easiest and fastest way to fix this is to not require the wearing of masks.   Maybe only wear a mask while stationary and unable to social distance as long as it doesn't affect your job.  TSA does give an option to not have to wear a mask if it is a safety concern as stated in the TSA website for the Executive Order. So my suggestion is to make the determination that due to a safety risk; the safety guidelines need [to] be changed to make masks optional on the individuals choice; depending on the job he or she is involved in due to the reasons stated above.

column121: Aircraft X was an air return back into ZZZ; for the standby display cool fan malfunction causing the display screens to overheat. This aircraft was ferrying to ZZZ1 for a repair. During troubleshooting it was decided that the problem could be relays K7HK and K11HK in JB2. The relays were replaced per the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) CH24/ESPM (Electrical Standard Practices Manual) and did not fix the problem. The next likely part was the avionics cooling control panel; it was replaced per AMM CH21 and did fix the problem. Because I had removed JB2; a retest had to be performed per the AMM CH24. The first half of this complex task was done in the hangar. The second half requires the engines to be ran. Everything was checking out good per the AMM; until the final engine start. During the start sequence on the LH (Left Hand) engine everything seemed to be normal; then I received an APU Overtemp red warning message which distracted me from watching the LH engine parameters. After the APU Overtemp message cleared I noticed the LH engine ITT (Interstage Turbine Temperature) at 998 degrees. I immediately put the LH thrust lever to fuel cutoff and motored the engine until the ITT was below 120 degrees. The MDC (Maintenance Diagnostic Computer) engine exceedance history showed the LH engine to be at 1110 degrees for 10.6 seconds. This is the first time I have ever encountered 2 overtemp events or 2 red warning indications at the same time while working one of our aircraft. I was working hard to get this task done so the crew could move the aircraft yet that day; as they were standing by in the hangar to depart after repairs were completed. I must admit I did feel pressured and hurried; however I did complete the retest task per the AMM; with everything checking satisfactory. As for the engine hot start event; I really regret it happening. It seems like it was one of those situations that does not occur together all that often. I felt I was distracted and was task overloaded for maybe a second or two which played a factor in this unfortunate event.

We then entered the fuel stick numbers into the fuel stick calculator where we determined the total fuel added to tank #3. We got approximately 36;600 lbs of fuel. We then went to the maintenance office and consulted with our lead. We had determined that the fueler had shorted us on the fuel load for fuel tank #3. We then called to have an additional 3;000 lbs of fuel added to fuel tank #3. Once the additional fuel was added to fuel tank #3 we verified this on stick #6 multiple times by both Name 1 and myself. Once this was all done we discussed with the flight crew the error that occurred with the first fuel load and the addition 3;000 lbs added to fuel tank #3 to give us a total of 40;000 lbs of fuel for fuel tank #3. They were content with this and after deicing the aircraft we pushed them off the gate. Once the aircraft departed; I gave the log sheet to my lead Name 2 to enter into workbench. He had entered it as was written. During the last fuel upload to tank #3 I made a correction to the log page indicating the new stick indications for sticks 6 and 7 giving us a total fuel load in tank # 3 of 40;000 lbs. The engine flameout I feel needs to be investigate further to determine if there was something that we could have done to prevent this.

column121: On Date there was an unfortunate damage to the Right Horizontal Stabilizer of Aircraft X. This damage drove Safety Bulletin on Date 1; which suggested a breakdown in communication as the root cause of the damage. However; most technicians (and supervisors) believe the real root cause of this damage was caused by the inability to use the correct equipment to accomplish the task at hand due to [the] Stores Department using both sides of this bay as staging and storage for their various equipment and items (tires; crates of all types and sizes; stacked at heights of over 10 feet in some instances). The work to be accomplished was on the right hand wing tip but because of all the equipment on the ground a small 35 feet JLG or widebody lift could not be used; instead a much larger JLG was necessary; positioned much further away; resulting in contact/damage to the right horizontal stabilizer. If this was a one off; the technicians probably would not have as much heartburn but this issue of stores using Bay 3; one of our prime widebody aircraft bays; as a storage has been going on for years and has resulted in other aircraft damages in the past.  This has been a well-documented and hot topic of discussion in ZZZ meetings; crew briefings; safety team raising it with messages; every level of management has been made aware of this over the years.  Sadly; the situation is getting worse instead of better.At our latest ZZZ meeting Date 1; a supervisor questioned the findings of the investigation stating that in his experience working the service center; he felt the stores equipment was more of a causation factor than the loss of communication. The reply from another member of management 'I am not aware of this being an issue'. Another participant suggested there was a lot of documentation but was told 'we can look into it and maybe build a case to get the stores equipment moved'. Since the damage; this stores equipment problem has been highlighted at the daily crew briefings and what is glaring to most techs since this damage is the fact that not only has nothing been done to mitigate the issue; it has actually gotten worse since the latest damage. This aircraft has been out of service now for almost 3 weeks; (if we are to believe the finance people when they tell us that a wide body generates X money on average a day); that's a costly stores area; just looking at it from that perspective!The unfortunate reality is in the event of a damage the technician is grilled in the investigation; sent for drug and alcohol testing; always made to feel at fault; always told it was self-induced pressure; and of course have their records pulled showing they signed off a specific training course; maintenance & engineering bulletin; awareness class etc. I have examples of this from many investigation reports.  I'm filing this report because the front-line mechanics don't want to for fear of repercussions if they did.  Sure; there are many human factors that come into play when incidents like this happen but when you look at it; this is not complacency on the part of the mechanics. There are real pressures to get these aircraft in and worked in BAY 3 and we crutch the system on a daily basis because of these pressures.  My question; how is Company living up to their values of safety always being #1 when this issue has been ignored for years despite the attention and spotlight?What is staggering to most; weeks after the latest very costly damage the situation is actually worse. The only answer could be; if you investigate and find the root cause that suits; then of course it will be impossible to mitigate and address the real root cause! I won't gain any friends for pointing this out but this issue needs to be addressed. It is our responsibility; from safety; to Management; coworkers etc.; to do the right thing; provide a safe work environment; which helps keep us all safe from injury and our assets from being damaged. We owe it to each other and ourcustomers. At this juncture this needs to be a priority from senior leadership because constant suggestions and concern from the floor have hit a brick wall and frankly we on the front line don't have the authority to fix the problem.

column121: I was called to assist in an aircraft spill situation on an A300 aircraft. I arrived as the First Responder was finishing up. I initiated the spill form and another AMT (Aircraft Maintenance Technician) documented the spill in the aircraft logbook. The aircraft had been in ZZZ since about midday and the spill was reported by the unload crew. The aircraft arrived with no containers in the aft lower compartment where the spill was located so a determination as to the source of origin for the spill would not be possible. The aircraft had operated [two] previous flight legs. The spill affected all areas of both the LH side and RH side outboard positions 5 through position 6. The responder said the spill was a 'mild' alkali and that he had used gray spill pads to try to absorb and clean up the unknown material. He said that a sample should be sent out to positively identify the substance. I documented this on the spill form which I completed down to the corrective action field. I inquired as to obtaining an [reference number] but there seemed to be a hesitancy to issue one and the spill form seemed to be met with the same response. The responder showed me the reference material that he used and stated that sodium bicarbonate could be used to clean up the unidentified spill. I informed both him and several on site Supervisors that since it had been identified as an alkali; the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) Chapter 5 procedures (as per the GMM) would take precedence for any cleanup actions. It appeared that they wanted to load the aircraft but sometime later; the aircraft was ultimately removed from service. I later spoke briefly to the incoming supervisor prior to my leaving my shift for the day and mentioned the spill form which needed the [reference number] and remaining entries after corrective actions were completed. The following day I pulled the history and saw that the log item had been cleared and noted that there was no deferral for a spill on the aircraft. Since I had initiated the spill form; I was concerned and called Company and asked if they had a copy of the completed form. They controller looked but could not find one. I reached out to the [records department] who had the applicable log page but no attached spill form. I inquired as to whether the form had possibly already been scanned and the log page was there but the spill form was not to be found. I informed my Supervisor of my concerns. I understand the GMM (General Maintenance Manual) procedure directs that once the area has been cleaned and a visual inspection accomplished by the AMT; no further action is required but there is more to that procedure. GMM spill response procedures cover roughly two pages and are fairly specific regarding spills determined to be an alkali; a spill that does not have a known source and the requirement for a deferral for a reinspect of the spill area at a later date. The GMM also provides guidance for the disposition of the aircraft spill form. I went upstairs to my manager's office and asked the questions regarding this procedure with the GMM in hand. The response that I got was that the spill was cleaned up by a [company name] vendor that we pay good money for (cleanup service) and at that point; the aircraft spill form is no longer necessary and that is the end of it as far as I was to be concerned. I mentioned that his answer is not in line with what the GMM says. My ultimate concern is for the aircraft and for the AMT's who signed the logbook if any part of this process was misrepresented to them in the name of getting the aircraft back into service. Hopefully this is not the case. The ZZZ Aircraft Hazardous Material Spill Flow Chart; the GMM and the Aircraft Substance Spill Form are very specific with the responsibilities for spill events such as this. It seems like every spill event in ZZZ is like the first time with decisions being made on the fly.

column121: ZZZ MX (Maintenance) called and informed that the LH eng took 19 Quarts. MX inspected the inside and outside of the eng cowl and eng; tailpipe; inlet and behind fan blades with no evidence of a leak. The inbound crew did not write up a problem with the oil QTY. We reviewed AHM (Automated Health Monitoring) report with was posted inflight an hour prior to landing and showed good QTY and oil pressure and no high oil temp. We reviewed the oil service screen in work bench and no servicing has been done for a while which showed no oil consumption issues. We asked to MX service the oil tank and run the engine; no leaks found and a good oil gulp at start which tells us the tank is not over serviced. We put the engine oil qty on MEL for two reasons one that the oil qty transmitter was giving false readings and MX may have thought when they checked the gauge in the cockpit that the engine was full and that's why the oil screen also showed very little oil servicing of the engine. Second reason is that by putting the engine on MEL that forces the mechanic to check oil at the tank and document it. There for showing if we truly have an oil consumption problem. We monitored the take off and looked at the takeoff report and it showed good oil qty and pressure. About an hour later we got a report of the engine having high oil temp. We looked at AHM; it did show a high oil temp with oil Qty and pressure good. On post landing at ZZZ1 MX did a look at the engine and once again no leaks found. With the oil temp high that's when we asked them to pull the master oil chip detector and it had metal shavings on it. With the oil temp over limit that requires an engine change.I'm not sure we can prevent this kind of failure this was a really oddball problem we have not seen before. I think we were a victim of a failing lube and scavenge pump or gearbox the oil may have been hiding in the gearbox. If we were to do this again I may have asked MX to do a high power run instead of just an idle run; But it may not have shown the problem.
