column121: While performing a Phase 1 inspection on Aircraft X at ZZZ under Work Order #XXXXX; I observed that the aileron trim cables were loose and dragging along the bottom of the wing. Attempts to adjust the cables to achieve proper tension and clearance were unsuccessful. I determined that the cables were stretched beyond serviceable limits and directed that they be replaced.Mechanic Person A completed the cable replacement under Line #51. Following installation; the trim control exhibited binding. I suspected the actuator to be the cause and instructed Person A to replace it under Line #59. After the actuator was installed; I asked Person A to perform travel checks. He reported that the checks were complete and that they're good."As the RII (Required Inspection Item) mechanic; I inspected the safety wire and verified control knob movement. No binding was present at that time. I then signed off the RII for Lines 51 and 59; along with the remainder of the Phase 1 inspection package.On Day 0; at approximately XB:00 local time; Aircraft X departed ZZZ for the scheduled ZZZ1/ZZZ2 feeder flight. Shortly after takeoff; the aircraft returned to ZZZ. Upon taxi-in and shutdown; the pilot reported that the aileron trim was operating in reverse--right trim input resulted in left trim movement; and left trim input resulted in right trim movement. Maintenance subsequently confirmed that the aileron trim system was functioning opposite to normal operation.On Day 0; at XA:27 local time; I departed ZZZ on Flight ABCD en route to ZZZ1. During the initial climb; passing through approximately 500 feet AGL; the aircraft began an uncommanded roll to the right. I applied left control wheel input along with left aileron trim; however; the right roll became more pronounced while in IMC conditions.Maintaining runway heading; I then applied right aileron trim; which successfully leveled the wings. I immediately contacted Tower and advised that I was returning to the airport. I initiated a shallow left turn and reduced power to begin a descent; requiring minimal control wheel input.I broke out of the overcast at approximately 400 feet AGL into 1¼ miles visibility in mist. I advised Tower that I had the airport in sight. The controller responded; "I have you in sight--no need to reply." I landed without incident.Cause:The aileron trim system malfunction on Aircraft X was caused by a reversal of the aileron trim cables during maintenance performed as part of the Phase 1 inspection at ZZZ. The original trim cables were found to be stretched and improperly tensioned; prompting their replacement under Line #51. During reinstallation; the new cables were inadvertently routed in reverse. Although subsequent binding led to the replacement of the trim actuator (Line #59); post-maintenance checks did not detect the reversal.The reversed cable configuration resulted in opposite directional input from the cockpit trim control--right trim input produced left trim movement and vice versa. This condition was not identified during post-maintenance functional checks or RII sign-off. The issue was discovered in flight on Day 0; prompting a safe return to ZZZ. Maintenance confirmed the reversal upon inspection.The root cause of the incident was the incorrect routing of the aileron trim cables during installation; compounded by insufficient verification of correct directional control function during post-maintenance checks.Looking back; I did not verify the direction of trim movement during the RII. The cables were not clearly labeled inside the wing root; and the reversal was not caught during rigging or travel checks. I take full responsibility for the oversight and support the corrective actions being implemented to prevent this from happening again.Suggestions: Mandatory Direction Check During RII.Require all RII inspectors to verify correct directional movement of flight controls after any cable or actuator replacement. This should be a documented step; notjust a verbal confirmation.Improved Cable Labeling.Label aileron trim cables and rigging points inside the wing root with clear; durable identifiers to prevent reversal during installation.Two-Person Verification.Implement a structured two-person check for all flight control rigging tasks. One mechanic performs the work; and a second independently verifies correct routing and control direction.Stand Down Protocol.Support the rollout of the Maintenance Safety Stand Down feature in the company app. Mechanics should feel empowered to pause work and ask for help without hesitation when something doesn't feel right.Workload Management.Reassess workload distribution at ZZZ. Time pressure and limited staffing contributed to reduced verification discipline. Shifting some tasks to other bases could help reduce risk."

column121: On the day of the event; I was assigned to Terminal Safety on the move crew. Aircraft X was being towed to Gate XX. I was not the pickup truck driver. Our team parked the pickup truck used for crew transportation in what was believed to be outside the sterile area.I was assigned responsibility for the left wing. As the aircraft approached; I signaled the location of the lead-in line and then repositioned myself to the left wing. I maintained continuous visual awareness of the left wingtip and the tail; as the tail was still positioned in the roadway.When the aircraft stopped to allow the marshaller to dismount the vehicle; I observed that the pickup truck appeared to be too close to the #1 engine. I immediately attempted to activate the TTWS (Tow Team Warning System) by pressing the wand buttons. When no response occurred; I ran toward the front of the aircraft while continuing to signal STOP and repeatedly attempting to activate the TTWS. Due to my position and distance; I was unable to get the tug driver's attention in time.Despite these actions; I was too far from the aircraft to prevent the collision between the aircraft and the pickup truck.I believe the damage resulted from inconsistent sterile area markings at Gate XX. The narrow-body and wide-body markings are not clearly differentiated; unlike at other gates such as Gate: XY; XZ; and XA; which contributed to the chain of events leading to the accident. Additionally; the TTWS did not function; further contributing to the incident. The company has been notified multiple times of ongoing TTWS issues; and corrective action has not yet been completed.Cause:  Sterile area markings are confusing and inconsistent they don't really differentiate narrow body or wide body compared to other gates like XA; XZ and XY also the TTWS system failed to go off which would've prevented the accident from happening.  Suggestions:  ZZZ operations has to correct sterile area markings and TTWS issues need to be fixed immediately that's our only line of defense against these types of accidents.

column121: All Maintenance; Line and Heavy; Leads; Inspectors; Engineering; SMS.What this is about: Freeze spray is used to test heaters on gray water drain lines in various aircraft locations; including confined and low-airflow areas. Found out last night the threat of suffocation is real.The hazard: Per the manufacturer's Safety Data Sheet; this spray is a liquefied gas that: displaces oxygen; vapors are heavier than air; [and] can cause rapid suffocation with no warning. Boeing Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) allows the spray but does not warn about oxygen displacement.Where this gets risky: Cargo compartments; bilge/underfloor areas; and any closed or poorly ventilated space.Bottom line: You can pass out before you know there's a problem.Suggested resolution: Bulletin: Do not use freeze spray without ventilation. Open doors or establish airflow first. Use minimum amount. If airflow can't be ensured; use another method. Dizziness or shortness of breath = stop and get out. Remember: AMM approval does not remove SDS hazards. Safety first.

column121: During installation of an APU into Aircraft X; both the left aft mount attached to the aircraft and the Apu mount received damage. After reviewing the damage it was clear what caused it; but during installation it was not easily seen how to avoid it. Maintenance Manual 49-11-00-400-802 part J-step 3 (c) 1-5 gives instructions on how to tighten the nuts once the Apu has been hoisted into place on the mounting bolts. During step 5 while torquing the nuts; the flange on the Apu aft mount cone bolt (attached to aircraft) was snapped off. The torque was set to 400 inch lbs and the process was being supervised by Quality Control. While torquing there was very little resistance; and any felt was assumed to be the weight of the APU resting on the nuts. What had occurred was before torquing; the flange on the cone bolt was not properly aligned with the mating surface on the APU mount. It appears that normally when the APU is hoisted to the bolts; the flange(which rotates freely); makes contact with a fin on the APU mount; which forces the flange into the correct orientation and self aligns. This particular bolt did not move freely without the aid of a tool; and the flange got caught on the fin on the APU mount(instead of rotating into correct orientation). When torque was applied to the nut the flange was bent to the point of breaking and it also left indentations on the APU mount. The Maintenance Manual does not give clear instructions to make sure the flange is lined up properly before torquing the nut. In hindsight it is easy to look at the mount and flange and see how it should be installed but during hoisting and torquing from below the APU; it is not.Suggestions:  Add additional instructions in the Aircraft Maintenance Manual to beware of the flange orientation before torquing; making sure the bolt has aligned itself properly.

Mounting fatigue and stress from the previous nights; and arriving later in the evening to my aircraft; may have led to a lack of attention to detail. He also stated that ZZZ is not allocated the APN-92 probe. It was determined by other management personnel that since ZZZ had accomplished the inspection in accordance with the appropriate job card the inspection results were considered acceptable. The preferred probe as called out in the job card "equipment" section is not being used consistently at stations assigned to accomplish the inspection.Suggestions: Revise the job card to only allow specific probes and assure the required probes are available at each station that accomplishes this task. Require specific findings i.e. current or propagated dimensions of any damage during follow up inspections be included on any update. Not just use statements such as "recheck accomplished;" "inspected and found to be in limits;" etc."

column121: While accomplishing a-check on gear assignment for Aircraft X found previous improper maintenance done to both wheel well Emdp case drain filters system A and system B for hydraulic case drain filter system servicing done on task card or by Aircraft Maintenance Manual B737ng. For system A the holes were broken on the module and the previous technician installed the safety wire to the adjacent hydraulic line instead of replacing the module and the safety was poorly installed using 20 thousand safety wire. For system B; the previous technician installed the packing that resides inside the module on top of the filter bowl; while correcting the issue; I found the filter not secured to the module because the filter o-rings was installed incorrectly as well not installed in the o-rings slot but sitting on top of the filter; the safety wire was installed loosening and I was able to remove the filter bowl by hand. I corrected both issues by replacing the module and replacing the filters; packings and backup rings. Reference logbook deferral sheet XXXXXXX and XXXXXXY. This is the fifth time in two weeks I have noticed in the wheel well of case drain bowls being safetied to hydraulic lines and second time of the packing being installed on the outside of the bowl and not inside the unit.Cause:  In these instances I was on walkaround while on A-check and pointed it out to the individuals on gear which we corrected these issues; but for Aircraft X; I was on gear and did not have task cards assigned to service these case drain filters. Suggestions:  I feel that the company needs to have a junior mechanic program for individuals who are fresh out of A&P school with no previous experience working at any airline. This is a recipe for disaster and a huge safety hazard. When I started in aviation over XX years ago; we had a ojt program where you were paired with a senior technician and had to accomplish ojt before graduating to the floor. Before arriving at Air Carrier X I worked at the Regional airlines and did contract maintenance heavy jet until I was hired at Air Carrier X. There cannot be inexperienced technicians out on the floor without any prior airline experience with only school under their belt which is the basics. Their should be a minimum of two years mandatory as a junior technician paired up with a senior technician for safety reasons. In the past years with Air Carrier X hiring people fresh out of school; I have seen too many things which can lead to a safety issue; whether the inexperienced individual doesn't ask; doesn't care; or just does a job any type of way without consulting and referencing the aircraft maintenance manual. Something has to be done because I see a huge safety issue and I don't want anything to happen; I am very worried about the lack of experience from people fresh out of school without at least 2 years of hands on experience working at a FBO or airline.                              The low seniority resides on night shift; this is where I feel 85% of the maintenance is being taken place; this is also where new hires mostly fresh out of school are placed due the airlines demand to hire anyone due to the shortage of mechanics and future demands. An airline must hire qualified and experienced technicians or have in place a junior technician program. Since around the time of retiring some of our fleet; the overall workmanship; quality; professionalism of maintaining our aircraft has hugely diminished; this is what I see; this is what a passenger see's as well because our interiors of our aircraft is a reflection of our maintenance program to any passenger that flies on our aircraft.  It is absolutely necessary that a junior program be set in place before senior mechanics with great experience; military experience that has served for this company for over 40 years pass down their knowledge before its too late so that the incoming generation of technicians understand the expectancy level and the requirements of their job qualification as well as performance to be able to provide safety and a quality product to our passengers and the many people we serve across the world. A lot of work is needed in our maintenance program regardless of how much profit we make. In the end; I don't want to hear something on the news and then the company reacts. it will be too late!  I also don't want to see aircraft get damaged or someone get hurt which recently I've seen many close calls. With this being said; we have to do better when it come to safety and quality whether in house or outsourced technicians that provide maintenance to our aircraft.

column121: On day 0 I was put on the engine change crew to continue with the remove & replace of #2 engine on aircraft x. My first job was to apply the protective coating on the bottom of the aft engine mount due to corrosion that was found during the after removal of engine lower pylon inspection. Upon first application of the primer i noticed that the bottom outboard mating surface of the aft engine mount had in my opinion a substantial amount of pitting. I ceased operation and notified the inspector of my finding. The inspector did a visual of the area and told me that it was ok to continue the application of the second coat and the area was within limits.the initial found fault of corrosion found during the engine inspection was already documented and signed off as removed corrosion per the applicable aircraft maintenance manual (amm). I initially took his word for it and continued because i was just coming to a somewhat extensive and lengthy job and assumed that everything had been researched and performed per any applicable amm or structural repair manual (srm). While waiting on the paint to cure enough for work to be performed i did start research in the srm to look for limitations on corrosion in certain areas. I found a few items in the srm that went over engine mounts and brought it to the inspectors attention. There were some limits that we went over and came to agreement that .020 was a max allowable limit on certain areas. I do recall looking mainly in the srm i did also eventually look in the amm and found a ref for the inspection of the aft engine mount. At this point i was still taking into consideration that he is a quality control inspector and that he has  more extensive training in limits and expectations of repairs of damaged areas on the aircraft as well as the experience of seeing discrepancies like this on a more regular basis. After we had hung the engine and installed engine mount bolts i looked back at the task card and noticed that the engine install( the task the inspector said was used for the inspection) referenced the removal of corrosion amm for both the inspection of the lower pylon fwd and aft fittings as well as the lower longeron and the remove corrosion if found item. In my opinion i could not see how you can use a reference to remove corrosion as a reference for doing an inspection. I went to the amm for the inspection of the aft engine mount and found that it calls out for the removal of the mount itself to do the inspection. I then brought it up to everybody i believe and pressed the issue until we were instructed to remove the engine by our manager. We subsequently found a substantial amount of corrosion in the pylon bolt holes at the point where i went off shift. I was questioned as to why; if i believed that the pitting corrosion was not in limits then why would i assist in the engine install up to the point of where i called for the removal. The only answer i can give is that i was trusting of the judgement of my fellow mechanic/inspector but for my sake and the safety of the aircraft/lives i was still going to continue research until i was either satisfied with the inspectors signoff or i found documented evidence that disputed him. I was concerned about flight safety and my fellow union members that were working on it and was willing to call for the engine removal no matter what step of the install we were on. column121: On Day 0; we had Aircraft X enter RON (Routine Overnight) with pump 2A on MEL and pump 2B requiring removal due to high time. The mechanics removed and installed the two pumps; and the aircraft flew to ZZZ. When the aircraft landed; they noticed fuel leaking from the belly of the aircraft. ZZZ says fuel pump 2B canon plug was not connected and pump 2A was missing an O-ring  which caused the leak. The mechanics states that the pump comes with o rings already pre-installed and that they remember connecting the canon plug.  Per the Maintenance Manual the fuel pumps are not RII (Required Inspection Item) since they are internal tank components which internal tank components do not require leak check and no item under ATA 28 requires RII for operational check (system check). The Maintenance Manual states that the preinstall and leak check on fuel tanks panels is RII. I watched one of the techs prep the panels and installed new o rings and lubricants that the AMM (Aircraft Maintenance Manual) called for. I did an area check prior to panels being installed to verify no tools or unwanted materials were inside of the tanks. I then stayed nearby to watch the install of the panels and watched the panels be torqued. After; the mechanic finished torquing the panel I verified each bolt by physically going over every bolt with the torque wrench. I then watched the leak check for the panels and after transferring fuel into the center tank there were no leaks noted from the fuel panels.We have one specific mechanic that works here that is a danger to our hanger and he needs to be spoken to because he is constantly messing things up.Suggestions:  Mechanics need to do a better job when it comes to working on the aircraft. They need to make sure they are following the AMM tasks references to ensure this does not happen again.
column123: On Day 0 I was the lead for RON (Routine Overnight) Aircraft X. The aircraft required fuel pump 2A and 2B to be changed for an MEL and suggested for high time respectively. I assisted in the installation of these pumps. When installing pump 2B I failed to connect the cannon plug that allows the pump to operate. Later on; when the ops check failed; it was documented on the paperwork and due to a lack of time the pump was placed on MEL. Following a clear to close/area safety check by an inspector; the panels were installed by another mechanic on shift. When the aircraft landed in ZZZ; fuel was noted to be leaking from the aircraft on the ground and was brought into maintenance. They found that pump 2A was leaking due to a missing O-ring on the cannon plug that separates the tank from a dry area. These pumps come from stock with an O-ring preinstalled; as pump 2B had. Before leaving the hanger; a leak check had been performed and no fuel was noted to be leaking. I believe the person performing the leak check on the ground may not have noticed the leak because it was not coming from the panels being inspected.Cause: Attempting to meet deadlines and failing to properly double check/inspect work.Suggestions:  Inspect parts from stock for damage or missing components prior to installation. Perform more thorough area checks and double check work prior to installation of panels.

column121: On Day 2; I was assigned to build Pratt & Whitney 4060 HPT (Hight Pressure Turbine) module. There were three cardboard boxes stacked on a wooden pallet. The lowest box contained the T2 rotating airseal; the middle box contained the T1 outer airseal; and the top box contained the T2 retaining plate. The boxes were not secured to the pallet; which has not been an issue in the past.Previously; on Day 0; I had opened the top box containing the T2 retaining plate (P/N XXXXXX); installed the plate and placed the empty box back on top of the other two. On Day 2; I opened the box containing the T1 outer airseal; visually inspected the part and noticed an area on the edge that was dented and had raised metal. Looking closer I noticed it was cracked. Inspection looked at the damage; rejected the part and placed the item on pending Engineering review. On Day 3; I removed the bottom box containing the T2 rotating airseal and immediately noticed a grey powder near the edge of the part. The edge had what appeared to be a dent approx. 2' long and a rough; jagged area about the same length as the dent. Inspection looked at the damage; rejected the part and placed the part on pending Engineering review. It appears that both parts suffered impact damage with a hard surface; probably concrete. All three items were made serviceable on different dates; so it is unlikely that they were damaged before or during their short stay in the stockroom. The logical conclusion is that the parts were pulled from stock; placed on the pallet and then fell off the pallet during transport from the stockroom to the build area. The cardboard box for the T2 rotating airseal had grey powder along the cut in the box; indicating the part came through the box; impacted; and then was pushed back into the box.Although having damaged parts is never a good thing; I am more concerned with the fact that someone knew these parts had fallen off the pallet and then placed them back inside the box and there was no follow-up to ensure the items were still serviceable. Was this accident brought to Management's attention or did the employee; fearing loss of his job; try and hide what happened? Once Inspection looked at the parts; it was immediately clear the parts were not serviceable; so I highly doubt anyone bothered to get Inspection involved. Furthermore; these parts still had serviceable tags on them; meaning the Inspectors who made them serviceable were placed in jeopardy by someone else's deliberate carelessness. Lastly; if I had not seen the damage and installed the parts; then my job would have been in jeopardy also. If I sound upset; it's because I am: hiding damaged parts is crossing the line and doing so endangers other employee's careers and puts our passenger's safety at risk.Suggested Resolution: The Company needs to do a better job communicating that damaged parts must be brought to the attention of Management; and Management must get Inspection or Engineering involved before proceeding. Early in my career it was drilled into me that you won't get fired for damaging a part; but you will get fired if you try and hide it. It appears the company is not doing a good enough job of ensuring this is well known amongst all employees.

column121: Day 23Statement on Aircraft X LH outboard flap maintenance.     On Day 0/1 Aircraft X was input at ZZZ for R3. My crew accomplished the base checklist in which we discovered; and I created found faults for.1)	LH wing OTBD (Outboard) upper split flap panel OTBD edge rubbing on bottom of aileron panel (Day 1)2)	LH wing OTBD flap at INBD (Inboard) actuator fairing has excessive play in fairing. (Day 1)     At the end of the shift; I gave a turnover about the damaged flap; and the actuator play at the fairing; to management during the shift turnover meeting and to the oncoming lead tech at the aircraft (as per SOP). As I recall now; I had even shown one of the on-coming managers the damaged flap and the play in the actuator at the inboard fairing.     On the evening of Day 7; our first night back I was informed at the lead turnover meeting; that the flap needed to be removed for evaluation since the ETIC (Estimated Time in Commission) was Day 10. My crew consisted of 5 technicians; 3 of which I assigned leading edge/fuel tank inspection tasks and the remaining 2 the task of removing the LH outboard flap for evaluation.     I provided the 2 technicians with the fault task card; maintenance manual procedure; and the illustrated parts manual for removal of the flaps. At which point my focus was then on the wing leading edges of which were found numerous cracks in the inner skins; and the inspection of the fuel tanks.     The flap was removed and I was told that there appeared to be damage to the actual hinge assembly; and that numerous spacers appeared to have been damaged by the play; and possibly some were missing. Me and the QC (Quality Control) tech looked over the flap and agreed with the techs that this did appear to be what was occurring. I then created a found fault (LH OTBD flap removed FOM (Maintenance Facility) Day 7) linking it to the actuator play fault. I was going to order the parts that appeared to be needed but had seen that the day shift lead tech had ordered everything but two bolts and two nuts on Day 6. At this time I ordered the bolts and the nuts. Again; at the end of my shift; I gave a turnover to management during the shift turnover meeting and to the oncoming lead tech at the aircraft (as per SOP). Also; at the end of my shifts for the remaining two days; I gave a turnover at the shift meeting stating all the parts that were on back order which were the shims and bolts.This was the last time that me and my crew had any interaction with Aircraft X until our meeting to discuss why the flap was removed the way that it was.Suggestions:  Management not wait 7 days to have technicians investigate a discrepancy if the due out time is in 10 days to where they are putting any shift/technician in a hurry up and get it done framework. Also when turnovers are given in meetings instead of the normal management shaking their heads and doing nothing; that they actually listen assigning someone in management to these large discrepancies to coordinate the way that these are worked from investigating the fault; through ordering of the parts; then verifying and expediting the acquisition of said parts instead of waiting to the last minute. Lead techs can only do so much with the resources that we have; and sometimes there are things that the resources available to management allow them to achieve at a more adequate/positive outcome.
column123: On Day 0; damage to an aircraft flap was identified; and the task was formally assigned on Day 6. With the aircraft scheduled for departure on Day 9; the timeline for assessment and corrective action was limited.Person A urgently requested assistance from myself and Person B to troubleshoot the unknown cause of the flap damage. Upon initial inspection; we identified noticeable play in the mount bolts connecting the flap surface to the outboard flap assembly.After careful evaluation; both technicians determined that a more detailed inspection of the mount bolt holes and associated bushings was required. This necessitated removal of the flap surface to allow for a thorough assessment. Following removal; excessive wear and elongation were discovered in the bolt holes; which had contributed to damage of the upper flap airfoil. Based on these findings; the flap surface hardware and bolt holes were found unserviceable.All hardware and shims were retained and temporarily reinstalled in their original positions following removal to preserve configuration integrity. A comprehensive turnover was conducted by Person C; both during shift handoff and at the morning meeting; ensuring the incoming team was fully informed of the worn flap surface attaching hardware and the status of the discrepancy.Suggestions:  A follow-up review found that the current maintenance documentation does not clearly address flap removal from the location used; and no cautions were identified regarding removal via the four attachment bolts in configurations that include factory-installed shims.To help prevent this from happening again; maintenance personnel will be reminded to ensure the task being performed is clearly supported by approved data and to seek additional guidance whenever procedures are unclear or not specifically addressed. This event will be forwarded for review; with consideration given to updating the maintenance manual to better define approved removal methods; highlight configuration considerations such as shimming; and include a note or reference outlining proper removal and reinstallation procedures when accessing the flap from this location. This event will also be shared with maintenance teams to reinforce the importance of confirming procedures prior to disassembly; especially when working under time constraints.

During installation of the new nozzle the mounting ears of the nozzle got bent due to an unseen misalignment of the nozzle.  It was found that either during removal of the old nozzle or during insertion of the new one that there is a tapered boss on the burner can internal to the engine that floats in a flange; this boss was shifted and causing the new nozzle to not correctly engage into the engine.  From the aft edge that is visible the nozzle was sitting flush with the engine case but it was lifted on the backside (fwd) edge where you couldn't see without a mirror.  The mounting nuts were run down and damaged the mount ears of the new nozzle during this process.  No damage occurred to the engine mounting boss. The nozzle was removed and after researching found that the floating tapered boss can be moved back into position and another replacement fuel nozzle was inserted without issue.Suggestions:  Add a warning note in the MX (Maintenance) manual to notate that the internal alignment of the floating tapered burner can boss can be moved if pushed on during removal/install causing the reinstallation of the nozzle to not align in its bore correctly.  Suggest a process to realign the tapered boss if it inadvertently gets shifted.

I preformed numerous additional gear swings not required per the maintenance manual.  I make a habit of doing this after a gear change as an extra level of safety.  If there is any problem with the extension and retraction system it needs to be known.  Aircraft X was released two days later and went to the gate.  After takeoff the gear failed to retract.  The NLG WOW sensor gap was determined to be the cause for the gear not retracting.I have adjusted many WOW proximity switches on the EMB-145 using both methods with no issues.  I am not really sure how this problem with the sensor adjustment occurred. I rechecked the gap after I completed the adjustment and it still measured good.Suggestion:  Although I would think that the results should be the same.  There are two different procedures for adjusting gear proximity switches. Possibly one procedure is more accurate then the other.

column121: Incorrect Hardware Stack-Up on LH Engine FWD Upper Mount BoltWe were performing a scheduled engine change and upon removal of the LH engine we found that the FWD Upper Mount Bolt was missing one of the two washers. AIPC (Aircraft Illustrated Parts Catalog) 71-21-01-01 calls out for 3 washers to be installed on this bolt. One countersunk washer against the head of the bolt and two flat washers on the other end under the nut. By only having one washer installed it is unlikely that the torque was done correctly and the cotter pin hole was not properly aligned with the cutout in the nut leaving it possible for the nut to back off.Cause: No idea other than lack of paying attention. On this job card these are the steps that reference the washers:Step #XX tells you to remove the washers (plural) from the upper mount and references you to Figure #XY for the picture.Step #XZ tells you to remove the washers (plural) from the lower mount and references you to Figure #XY for the picture.Step #XZ tells the inspector to examine the washers (plural) and references you to Figure #XA for the picture.Step #XB tells you to install the washers (plural) and references you to Figure #XY for the picture. There is also a Note that specifically calls out that there are two washers installed under the nut as illustrated in Figure XY.Step #XC tells you to install the washers (plural) and references you to Figure #XY for the picture. There is not a Note here but there is nothing saying that you can just remove one of those washers.We replaced all the FWD Upper and Lower mounting hardware (i.e. bolts; flat washers; countersunk washers; and bushings) and moved on with installing the new engine.I have no suggestions for this one
